Introduction:
Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and influenza are respiratory tract infections that may cause severe morbidity and mortality. COVID-19 has so far led to >7 million deaths since 2019 [ 1 ], while seasonal influenza or “flu” causes 290 000–650 000 deaths annually [ 2 ]. Although most episodes of COVID-19 or influenza do not require medical attention, their severity and case-fatality increase among individuals affected by chronic non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, metabolic, neurodevelopmental, liver, or hematologic diseases, as well as among those with immunosuppressive conditions or treatments (such as HIV, receiving chemotherapy or steroids, or malignancy) [ 2 , 3 ]. High-risk groups also include pregnant women and, for influenza, young children [ 4 ].

Vaccination is critical to the prevention of hospital admissions and deaths due to both diseases. Whereas the influenza vaccine has been available since the 1940s and its adoption by countries was gradual, the development and global deployment of COVID-19 took place rapidly from 2020 onwards, leading to >13.5 billion doses being administered [ 5 ]. Such a success story was made possible by unprecedented scientific collaborations, extensive prior research, and substantial public funding, which enabled vaccine development to be completed in record time while maintaining high safety standards. New versions of influenza and COVID-19 vaccines are regularly being developed as both viruses continue to circulate and mutate [ 6 ].

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends COVID-19 vaccination for all individuals, with booster doses recommended every 6–12 months for high-priority adults >50 years old [ 2 , 7 ] or who present comorbidities or immune deficiencies [ 8 ], health workers with direct patient contact, and children and pregnant women [ 9–11 ]. For influenza, WHO recommends annual vaccination for pregnant women, children aged 6 months to 5 years, people aged >65 years, people with chronic medical conditions, and health workers [ 2 ].

Flu vaccination has been offered in Brazil since 1999 [ 12 ]. In 2024, the Ministry of Health recommended the vaccine for all individuals aged ≥6 months to achieve universal coverage [ 13 ] rather than restricting immunization to priority groups, as was the case in the past. Yet, national vaccine coverage as of July 2024 had only reached 44% among priority groups (pregnant and puerperal women, older adults, children, and native people living in reservations), according to official data [ 14 ].

Brazil started COVID-19 immunization in January 2021, with the Ministry of Health recommending two doses for children <5 years of age and one dose for all others, except for immunocompromised persons, who should receive three doses. The recommendation also includes annual booster doses for priority groups such as Indigenous people and persons with comorbidity, and 6-monthly doses for immunocompromised people aged ≥5 years, pregnant or puerperal women, and persons aged ≥60 years [ 15 ]. Based on official data from 19 January 2021 to 22 March 2023, national coverage with at least one COVID-19 vaccine was 88%, while 82% were fully vaccinated with all recommended doses. The Johns Hopkins vaccine tracker estimated the one-dose coverage as 89%, with Brazil ranked fifth among Latin American countries [ 16 ].

COVID-19 vaccine coverage varies among the country’s regions, being lower in municipalities with lower education levels, higher proportions of Afro descendants, high income, and worse health service indicators [ 17 ]. Economic and educational inequalities in influenza vaccine coverage were also reported by some authors but not by others [ 18 , 19 ].

The nationwide EPICOVID19 study, conducted in Brazil in 2020, consisted of four repeated serological survey waves assessing the presence of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and focusing on monitoring the pandemic expansion in the country. The surveys were conducted in 133 sentinel cities in all 26 Brazilian states and the Federal District [ 20 ], by using probability sampling within each city. In 2024, the EPICOVID 2.0 study was implemented, using the same methodology, to evaluate the impact of the pandemic in Brazil, including measuring the coverage of COVID-19 and influenza vaccines. In addition to coverage, reported reasons for non-vaccination were studied, as were regional and socio-demographic inequalities in coverage levels.
Methods:
Methodological details of the EPICOVID 2.0 study are available in a companion publication [ 21 ].

### Study design and sampling

A nationwide survey in Brazil was conducted between 11 March and 3 June 2024 in 133 sentinel cities from the 26 Brazilian states and the Federal District. According to the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE), those cities were the most populated cities in the country’s 133 intermediary regions. Multistage sampling was employed. First, 25 census tracts were selected with probability proportionate to size in each sentinel city. Second, 10 households were randomly selected within each tract, using maps and household listings made available by the IBGE. Third, one individual was randomly chosen from a list of all household members and, in the case of refusal, a second individual was randomly selected. If this individual refused, then the interviewer proceeded to the next household on the right side of the original house. The field team recorded refusals and household replacements.

### Data collection

Data were collected simultaneously throughout the country by a team of surveyors working for a company with substantial experience in previous surveys commissioned by the Brazilian Ministry of Health. A smartphone app was used in data collection and uploading [ 21 ].

The sampled individuals answered a face-to-face questionnaire. Vaccine uptake was assessed through the questions “Are you vaccinated against COVID-19?” and “Are you vaccinated against flu?”. For COVID-19, those who answered yes were also asked how many doses they took (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or more). We described the prevalence of ≥1 dose, ≥2 doses, and ≥4 doses. Interviewers also asked about how the information received on the COVID-19 vaccine affected the respondent's attitude (“avoids the vaccine,” “indifferent,” or “seeks the vaccine”).

Information on explanatory variables included the geographic region of residence (North, Northeast, Southeast, South, or Center-West) and socio-demographic variables: self-reported skin color (in Portuguese: branco, preto, pardo, amarelo, or Indigenous; respectively White, Black, Brown, Asian, and Indigenous), sex (female or male), age in years (0–19, 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, 80+), and years of schooling (0–4, 5–8, 9–12, 13+). Four groups of religious affiliation were included in the analyses: none, Catholic, evangelical, and others. To assess the socioeconomic position of households, we calculated a wealth index based on principal component analysis of a set of household characteristics and assets (computer, internet access, color television, air conditioning, motor vehicles, cable television, number of bathrooms, and number of residents per bedroom), similar to what is done for Demographic and Health surveys [ 22 ].

### Data analysis

Initial analyses described the sample in terms of the geographic and socio-demographic variables and vaccine coverage. For COVID-19, three variables were calculated (≥1 dose, ≥2 doses, and ≥4 doses), while, for influenza, the variable referred to having ever been vaccinated (yes or no). In the unadjusted analyses, vaccine coverage was stratified according to the explanatory variables, with point estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) being presented. Significance was by tested using chi-squared tests for heterogeneity and for linear trends in proportions.

Poisson regression models were also run to estimate the prevalence or coverage ratios of COVID-19 and influenza vaccines according to the explanatory variables. First, an unadjusted model was run, followed by a multivariable regression in which explanatory variables were gradually included according to a postulated hierarchical model with three levels: (i) geographic region and demographic variables (skin color, sex, and age); (ii) socioeconomic (religious affiliation, years of schooling, wealth); and (iii) vaccine information. Further analyses explored intersectionalities between sex and four other explanatory variables: age, skin color, wealth index, and schooling. Poisson regression was then used to estimate the Wald test for the interaction terms.

We calculated the sampling weights to represent the target population by using data from the IBGE, which included population size, sex, age, and race/color for each city. Specifically, we considered the distribution of sex, age, and ethnicity for each of the 133 cities (based on the 2022 census) [ 23 ] and compared it with the same distribution in the EPICOVID 2.0 survey. The population size was also accounted for by dividing it by the number of interviews ( n = 250) conducted in each city. These quotients were then multiplied to calculate the final survey weights.

All statistical procedures were run on Stata 18. Sampling weights were accounted for by using the “svyset” command, with the city as the stratification variable and the census sector as the primary sampling unit. All subsequent analyses were conducted by using the “svy” command in Stata, which adjusted for the complex survey design by accounting for stratification, clustering, and within-city correlations.
Results:
The 33 250 interviews took place in 2024 (from 11 March to 3 June) in 133 urban areas. Of the initially contacted subjects, 7.5% refused to be interviewed and were replaced to complete 250 questionnaires per city. All results shown below were obtained from the weighted analyses, but unweighted results are also presented in the Supplementary materials and unweighted sample sizes in a companion paper [ 21 ].

Influenza vaccine coverage was 82.6% (95% CI, 81.6; 83.5) ( Fig. 1 ). Coverage with one or more doses of COVID–19 vaccines was 90.2% (95% CI, 89.5; 90.9). Two or more doses were received by 84.6% (95% CI, 83.8; 85.5) and four or more doses by 33.0% (95% CI, 31.6; 34.4) of the sample. Most individuals received three doses.

Table 1 shows the unweighted distribution of the sample. The region with the highest proportion of interviews was the Northeast (31.6%), followed by the Southeast (24.8%). Most of the sample were female (62.0%) and almost half reported having Brown skin color (49.4%). The modal schooling category was 9–12 years (47.2%) and, as expected, ∼20% of the individuals were classified in each wealth quintile. Catholic religion was the most prevalent (45.7%), followed by evangelicals (28.6%); the latter accounted for 5.1% of the sample, mainly spiritism (1.8%) and African rites (1.5%). Due to the information received during the pandemic, most individuals (76.1%) decided to pursue the vaccine, followed by 13.6% who opted to avoid it and 10.6% who reported being indifferent.

Table 1 also shows the breakdowns by categories of the explanatory variables of coverage with 1+, 2+, and 4+ doses of COVID-19 and 1+ doses of influenza. In the text below, we focus on patterns observed for two vaccine indicators, namely 4+ COVID-19 doses and influenza vaccination. Unless otherwise stated, observed differences were highly significant.

The Southeast region had the highest coverage for both vaccine indicators, while the North and Center-West had the lowest coverage. COVID-19 coverage tended to increase with age, ranging from only 6.0% in those aged 0–19 years to >60% after the age of 60 years. In contrast, differences in influenza vaccine coverage were less marked, showing a U-shaped pattern, being higher in younger and older individuals. Women were 8.7% points (pp) more likely than men to be vaccinated against COVID-19, but there were no differences for the flu vaccine. Regarding skin color, White people had the highest coverage against COVID-19 and Indigenous individuals had the lowest coverage, with a difference of 7.2 pp ( P = 0.038), whereas there were no ethnic differences for the influenza vaccine.

There was a wide educational gap in COVID-19 coverage, with a difference of >20 pp between the highest and lowest schooling categories. A U-shaped pattern was observed for influenza, with lower coverage in the two intermediate groups. A positive socioeconomic gradient was observed for COVID-19 coverage with a gap of 9.4 pp among the top and bottom quintiles, but no significant differences were observed in influenza vaccine coverage ( P = 0.468). In terms of religion, Catholics and a small group of other religions showed the highest coverage levels, whereas evangelicals and those without a religion showed the lowest coverage. Differences between Catholics and evangelicals were wider for COVID-19 (15.1 pp) than for influenza (3.2 pp).

As expected, there was a strong association between how the information received on COVID-19 affected individual attitudes towards vaccination. Coverage with 1+ dose was 96.7% ( Table 1 ) and with 4+ doses was 40.4% among those who decided to seek the vaccine, compared with 61.2% and 7.9%, respectively, among those who mentioned avoiding the vaccine. Information on COVID-19 vaccination also affected influenza coverage, with a difference of 20.3 pp between seekers and avoiders.

Table 2 presents the reasons for non-vaccination for each vaccine. For COVID-19, the main reason was the lack of belief in this vaccine (32.0%), followed by concern about harmful consequences (27.4%). For influenza, the main reason was they did not belong to a priority group for vaccination (28.4%). Other reasons than those described in Table 2 accounted for ∼27% of the answers regarding both vaccines. The main groups of such reasons included lack of access to functioning health services (26 responses), illness at the time of vaccination (23), lack of information and interest (18), personal or cultural objections (17), emotional or psychological barriers (10), and lack of family support (7).

The co-coverage analyses ( Fig. 2 ) showed that 76.7% of the sample received at least one dose of both vaccines, 13.5% received only the COVID-19 vaccine, 5.9% received only the flu vaccine, and 3.9% received neither.

Unadjusted analyses and adjusted models are presented in Table 3 for four or more doses of COVID-19 and Table 4 for the influenza vaccine. Corresponding results for one or more doses and for two or more doses of the COVID-19 vaccine are presented in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 . For each category of the explanatory variables, coverage ratios are presented. As expected, coverage ratios ( Table 3 ) show similar patterns according to explanatory variables, as did coverage levels ( Table 1 ). The first model included adjustments for region, age, sex, and skin color. The adjusted ratios for the first three variables are somewhat attenuated compared with the unadjusted results, but similar patterns remain ( P = 0.001 or lower). For skin color, differences were no longer observed after adjustment for region, sex, and age. The second model added schooling, wealth, and religion to the earlier model; despite attenuation, a positive dose–response association with schooling persisted, but the association with wealth quintiles was no longer stepwise or significant. Evangelicals had markedly lower coverage than the other religions ( P < 0.001) and the ratio to nonreligious individuals became even more marked in the adjusted (CR = 0.69) than in the unadjusted (CR = 0.86) analyses. In the last level of the hierarchical model, the effect of vaccine information was adjusted for all other covariates and the associations were similarly strong, albeit attenuated, compared with those observed in the unadjusted analyses.

Unadjusted coverage ratios for the influenza vaccine ( Table 4 ) were also compatible with the coverage levels reported in Table 1 , with significant differences observed only for the country region, schooling, religion, and effect of the information received. These differences persisted in the adjusted analyses, except for schooling, for which the association disappeared, and for age, which became statistically significant after adjustment ( P –0.012) with lower coverage among individuals aged 20–24 years. In general, coverage ratios were lower for the flu vaccine than for 4+ doses of the COVID-19 vaccine, partly because the possible range of ratios is mathematically limited for high-coverage outcomes.

Lastly, we investigated the presence of intersectionalities between sex and four explanatory variables: age, schooling, wealth, and skin color ( Supplementary Table S3 ). Interaction P levels for COVID-19 vaccines (four or more doses) were significant for age and skin color. Women tended to show higher coverage than men in virtually all subgroups. Still, coverage among men aged ≥70 years was ∼7 pp higher than for women in the same age group, and coverage among Asian men was 14.6 pp higher. In all other categories of age, schooling, and wealth, coverage tended to be higher among women, except for boys and girls aged <20 years, who had similarly low coverage levels.

There were no significant interactions between sex and other variables regarding the influenza vaccine, but, in the poorest quintile and among the Indigenous, women seemed to be more likely to be vaccinated, whereas the reverse was observed in the two wealthiest quintiles. Because CIs are wide, these findings must be interpreted cautiously.
Discussion:
Before discussing our results in detail, one should bear in mind the strengths and limitations of the study. This was the first nationwide study in Brazil with primary data collection measuring coverage with two priority vaccines. It was led by an experienced team that carried out a similar set of serological surveys in the same 133 cities during the peak of the pandemic, which resulted in the first description of how the pandemic moved around Brazil, with the highest initial antibody prevalence in the Amazon region and selected metropolises in the Southeast, then progressing to all country regions [ 24 ]. By relying on home interviews, the responders were not biased by access to telephones or the internet, and thus included individuals from different socioeconomic and ethnic groups. The final sample of >30 000 individuals allowed stratification by several explanatory variables with appropriate precision as well as analyses of intersectionalities.

The limitations of the study include restricting the sample to sentinel cities that constitute regional hubs, which are larger and tend to be more developed and have better health services than smaller cities. In addition, rural areas were not included; these account for ∼15% of the country’s population [ 25 ]. We could not collect information from household members who were either away at the time of the visit or refused to participate. Our sample had fewer children than was expected on the basis of the national population and White individuals and males were also underrepresented, possibly because these three groups were less likely to be at home when the visits took place. Weighting procedures were used to compensate for these differences in participation [ 21 ].

Our weighted analyses showed that COVID-19 vaccine coverage was 90.2% for at least one dose, 84.6% for at least two doses, and 33% for at least four doses. In March 2023, the estimate based on official vaccination records was 88.0% for one or more doses and 81.8% for two or more; these levels are very similar to those reported here, suggesting that the official figures, based on facility-reported doses, are highly reliable. According to the official data, Brazil ranked fifth among Latin American countries with the largest COVID-19 vaccination doses per 100 population [ 16 ].

However, the official estimates do not include coverage for four or more doses, which offer enhanced protection against evolving viral mutations. We opted for using coverage of at least four doses as the primary indicator of inequalities within the population, as more stringent health metrics tend to reveal disparities more effectively than less rigorous ones.

We found that influenza coverage was 82.6% in the whole sample, including doses received at any time in the past. Similar data from official sources are unavailable, as the reported coverage level of 44% corresponds to doses received in the past year and only for priority groups (pregnant and puerperal women, older adults, children, and native people living in reservations) [ 14 ].

An original finding resulted from the co-coverage analyses, showing substantial overlap between individuals who received both vaccines and revealing that only 3.9% of the sample failed to be immunized with either vaccine.

The Southeast region exhibited the highest vaccine coverage for both influenza and COVID-19, while the North and Center-West regions showed the lowest. Similar geographic gradients had been identified in earlier analyses of secondary data [ 17 , 26 ].

Several socio-demographic factors significantly influenced the vaccination rates. COVID-19 vaccine coverage increased with age, showing a particularly strong increase after age 60. This reflects the prioritization of older adults in the initial stages of the vaccine rollout in 2020, when uptake in this group was higher than for any other age range, which was soon followed by a reduction in mortality after age 60 [ 27 ]. In contrast, influenza vaccine coverage displayed a U-shaped pattern, with higher rates among younger and older individuals, in agreement with the priority given to young children and older adults [ 26 ].

Women demonstrated higher COVID-19 vaccination rates than men (8.7% age points higher)—a pattern that had also been reported in a secondary analysis of coverage with two or more doses [ 26 ]. In our study, the exception was among people aged ≥70 years, among whom male coverage was 7 pp higher than for females. The exact reasons for this inversion in the pattern are unclear, but a possible explanation is that older men are aware that COVID-19 deaths are more common for males than for females, and therefore may be more likely to seek the vaccine [ 28 ]. No sex gap was observed for the influenza vaccine.

White subjects exhibited the highest COVID-19 vaccination rates, while Indigenous individuals showed the lowest. Geographic [ 17 ] and individual-level [ 26 ] analyses of official data showed that White people were more likely to be vaccinated, with lower coverage among Black and Brown individuals. We were unable to find any nationwide studies of vaccination rates among Indigenous individuals with which our results could have been compared. Regarding the influenza vaccine, our results did not show any significant patterns.

Several authors have utilized national databases to show vaccine coverage inequalities according to education and wealth [ 17 , 26 , 29 ]. We found a substantial educational gap in COVID-19 vaccination rates, with a difference of >20%age points between the highest and lowest schooling categories. The positive gradient with schooling was attenuated in the wealth-adjusted analyses but remained significant. A positive wealth gradient existed for COVID-19 vaccination, which was no longer stepwise or significant in the adjusted model that included schooling as a covariate. In spite of the collinearity between the two explanatory variables, our results suggest that education is a stronger determinant of vaccine coverage than wealth.

The role of socioeconomic variables in determining influenza vaccination was unclear. Coverage showed a significant U-shaped association with schooling in the unadjusted analyses, which disappeared after adjustment. Wealth quintiles were not associated with flu vaccine coverage in any of the analyses.

The analyses of religious affiliation were particularly interesting. In a country that was once almost universally Catholic, the rapid expansion of evangelism has now reached ∼30% of the population. Evangelicals as a group tend to be strongly supportive of right-wing political parties, including the one led by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who is a spoken anti-vaccine person who states that he was never vaccinated [ 30 , 31 ]. Therefore, the findings that evangelicals are 16 pp less likely to be vaccinated against COVID-19 than Catholics is not surprising, and smaller studies in Brazil [ 32 ] and in England [ 33 ] pointed in the same direction. Moreover, lower vaccine coverage among evangelicals became even more accentuated after adjustment for covariates, including education and wealth, suggesting that the gap is not due to known confounding variables. Flu vaccine coverage, which is >80% in all subgroups, was still 3 pp lower among evangelicals than Catholics. The international literature suggests that religious affiliation, particularly Islam, is associated with lower childhood vaccine coverage [ 34 ] in some but not all countries, but we believe this is the first study to address evangelical affiliation.

The impact of information received regarding COVID-19 on vaccination decisions was significant, particularly in an era in which fake news is epidemic, including anti-science reports on the safety and efficacy of vaccines. Individuals who reported that the information received made them interested in seeking the COVID-19 vaccine had much higher coverage than those who interpreted the information as advice to avoid it. This pattern was unchanged by adjustment for covariates. Although the question was specific to information on the COVID-19 vaccine, a similar but less marked gradient was observed for the influenza vaccine, suggesting a spillover effect.

The main reasons for non-vaccination against COVID-19 were lack of belief in the vaccine (32%) and concerns about adverse effects (27.4%). For influenza, the most common—and understandable—reason was not belonging to a priority group (28.4%). Other factors contributing to vaccine hesitancy included limited access to healthcare services, illness at the time of vaccination, lack of information or interest, and cultural or psychological barriers.

Our results have direct implications for public health policies aimed at targeting specific subpopulations with renewed efforts to promote immunization, particularly ethnic and religious groups. The results also highlight the continued need to promote reliable, science-based information to the population and to strongly counteract false messages about vaccine safety and effectiveness.
